source_refs.note: Derived Units: a main subheading of 1.2 International System of Units, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 5-5.

blocks.text: Derived units are those units which depend on the base units. Some of the derived units are given in Table. 1.2. The units of plane angle and solid angle have also been included in the list of derived units since 1995.
In addition to base and derived units, the SI permits the use of certain additional units, including:

items: The traditional mathematical units for measuring angles (degree, arcminute, and arcsecond).
The traditional units for standard time are (minute, hour, day, and year).
The logarithmic units bel (and its multiples, such as the decibel).
Two metric units commonly used in ordinary life: the litre for volume and the tonne (metric ton) for large masses.
Two non-metric scientific units are atomic mass unit (µ) and the electron volt (eV).
The nautical mile and knot; units traditionally used at sea and in meteorology.
The acre and hectare, common metric units of land area.
The bar is a unit of pressure and it is commonly used as the millibar in meteorology and the kilobar in engineering.
The angstrom and the barn, units used in physics and astronomy.

blocks.alt: A vertical scale of mass in kilograms from 10⁻³⁰ at the top to 10³⁰ at the bottom, marked every five powers of ten. Beside it, from top to bottom: electron, proton, uranium atom, DNA molecule, cell, mosquito, book, car, oil tanker, Mount Everest, Earth and Sun.

blocks.text: The book prints the symbol of the atomic mass unit as µ (the Greek letter mu, which is the symbol of the prefix micro). The symbol of the atomic mass unit is u.
blocks.title: Book correction
Book correction
blocks.text: The printed chart places the proton near 10⁻²⁸ kg. The mass of a proton is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, where it is drawn above.
